problems.description: JWT is hand-rolled from hmac/hashlib/base64 primitives instead of a maintained library (PyJWT / flask-jwt-extended). The implementation is careful (constant-time compare_digest, explicit HS256 check, exp enforcement) but re-implements a standard with custom parsing/encoding that invites subtle bugs and duplicates library functionality.
No tests added for the new auth surface (register/login/protected-task routes, token expiry, bad tokens) even though test_app.py exists in the codebase; the diff touches only app.py (+0 files).

~150 lines of auth, token, and user-repository SQL are added directly to app.py while the codebase already modularizes (repositories.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py). Auth and user queries should live in a dedicated module/repository to match the emerging layering.

JWT_SECRET silently falls back to a hardcoded 'development-secret-change-me'; if deployed without the env var, tokens are forgeable. A fail-fast on missing secret would be safer, though acceptable for a dev/demo app.
require_auth performs a DB round-trip (SELECT id FROM users) on every protected request to confirm the user still exists; reasonable for revocation semantics but worth noting.

Measured convention score 0.67 (9 violations), but every listed violation except one (app.py PascalCase) is in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py), and the commit adds zero classes. The commit itself introduces no new naming violations; the low score reflects the pre-existing baseline. Flagging this discrepancy with the measurement.

strengths: Passwords are hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored in plaintext.
Row-level owner_id scoping on create/list/get tasks gives real multi-tenant data isolation.
Sound JWT hygiene: constant-time compare_digest, explicit HS256 alg check, iat/exp, and broad exception handling that fails closed on malformed tokens.
Forward-compatible SQLite migration: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS plus PRAGMA column check + ALTER TABLE for existing DBs, FK enforcement, and an index on owner_id.
Correct HTTP semantics (400/401/409/201) and consistent use of the existing get_db()/Flask `g`/decorator idioms.
commit_reviews.summary: A net improvement that delivers auth and per-user data isolation with solid crypto hygiene, but it hand-rolls JWT, crams the whole subsystem into app.py despite an existing repositories layer, and ships without tests.

problems.description: Register defaults email to username and the migration backfills email = username, so many stored 'emails' are not valid addresses and notification delivery will silently fail at send time; requiring email at registration would be cleaner.
Notification dispatch is fire-and-forget via .delay() with no retry/backoff or broker-connectivity handling; if Redis/Celery is down the transition to completed is lost with no visibility.
All tests monkeypatch .delay(), so the Celery wiring (task registration name, task_routes to the notifications queue, celery_config broker settings) is never exercised by the suite.

The 9 naming violations are largely Celery-convention false positives (broker_url/result_backend and celery_app are documented lowercase Celery style), and the repositories.py violation references a file not touched by this diff; the real new-code convention debt is small.

strengths: Edge-triggered notification only on the completed transition, with tests proving no duplicate sends on repeat updates
Safe schema evolution using PRAGMA introspection plus ALTER TABLE so pre-existing databases migrate cleanly
Proper task decoupling: standalone notification_tasks module, dedicated notifications queue via task_routes
Solid test coverage including duplicate-notification and non-completed edge cases, matching existing monkeypatch test style
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-integrated async notification feature that fits the app's existing patterns and is well-tested, with the measured convention score of 0.67 overstated by Celery-naming false positives.

problems.description: repositories.py introduces module-level constants that are not UPPER_CASE — the only new convention violation attributable to this commit

Repository instances are constructed inline per call (e.g. UserRepository(get_db).exists(...)) rather than once per request/context; harmless but slightly noisy, and open_database() is invoked repeatedly

strengths: Introduces a repository layer (TaskRepository/UserRepository) that cleanly separates data access from Flask view handlers, improving layering and testability
Replaces f-string-interpolated SQL column names with dict-based updates, removing dynamic SQL string construction
SonarQube delta confirms net improvement: +0 bugs, -1 smell, +0.0% duplications
Consolidates idempotent schema creation and migrations into initialize_schema(), removing duplicated PRAGMA/migration boilerplate
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive refactor that adds a repository layer and eliminates dynamic SQL while reducing smells (per SonarQube), though convention adherence stays moderate (0.67) — most of the 9 violations (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py) are pre-existing and only the non-UPPER_CASE constants in the new repositories.py are introduced here.

problems.description: Tests monkeypatch Flask-Limiter private internals (`limiter._storage`, `limiter._limiter`) instead of configuring `memory://` storage or `limiter.enabled=False`. This couples tests to library internals, duplicates the strategy config (FixedWindowRateLimiter), and — because a single shared MemoryStorage persists across the whole run against the 100/min default — can cause spurious 429 cross-test interference and flaky failures. (Later fixed in the worktree by disabling the limiter in the fixture.)

RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to Redis with no in-memory fallback, so a SQLite-backed service hard-fails every request if Redis is down. Consistent with the existing Celery/Redis dependency, but the app cannot degrade (a fallback was added only after this commit).

The single global default of 100/min also applies to /auth/login and /auth/register keyed by IP address — a shared NAT could lock out multiple legitimate users, and login endpoints typically warrant a much stricter dedicated limit than general API traffic.
A COUNT(*) runs on every page just to populate `total`, and the owner_id-only index means ORDER BY id DESC sorts the full filtered set — a composite (owner_id, id) index would serve both at scale.
The /tasks response contract changes from a bare array to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope — a deliberate, well-tested breaking change, but one that invalidates any existing consumers.

Mechanical convention score 0.67 (9 violations) reflects pre-existing issues in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, etc.); the introduced code itself is convention-clean.

strengths: Correct keyset (cursor) pagination using `LIMIT limit+1` has-more detection — avoids OFFSET pitfalls and scales on the PK index.
Input validation returns 400 for non-integer, zero, or >100 limit values and non-positive cursors.
Per-user rate-limit key derived from the bearer token with an IP fallback, plus proper 429 and Retry-After headers.
Pagination SQL lives in the repository layer, respecting the existing architecture and repository pattern.
Strong test coverage: ordering, multi-page cursor traversal, invalid-parameter matrix, per-user and per-IP rate limiting.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting session adding correct cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting with thorough tests, slightly marred by tests coupled to Flask-Limiter private internals (flakiness risk) and a hard Redis dependency for the rate-limit store.

compounding_issues: Session 2 hand-rolled JWT from hmac/hashlib/base64 primitives instead of using PyJWT/flask-jwt-extended; the S4 repository refactor never addressed the custom auth layer, leaving a security-sensitive reimplementation as standing debt

Session 2 added ~150 lines of auth, token, and user-repository SQL directly into app.py despite an existing modular structure; S4's repository extraction was partial, so the API routes still carry non-database logic and inline per-call repository construction

Session 3 dispatch is fire-and-forget Celery .delay() with no retry/backoff or broker-down handling, and every test monkeypatches .delay(), so task registration/routing is never exercised; this fragile async wiring compounds when S5 adds a Redis-backed rate limiter on the same infra

Convention score stayed flat at 0.673 across all five commits with the identical nine violations (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE) reappearing every session, indicating style debt was never remediated
Session 3 defaults user email to username, so stored 'emails' are not valid addresses and notification delivery silently fails at send time
key_decisions: Greenfield Flask + SQLite monolith in a single app.py (S1), establishing the module layout every later session built onto
Hand-rolled JWT authentication (constant-time compare_digest, explicit HS256, exp enforcement) rather than a maintained auth library (S2)
Celery + Redis async email notifications wired as fire-and-forget tasks on a dedicated notifications queue (S3)
Repository pattern extraction (TaskRepository/UserRepository) replacing f-string-interpolated SQL with dict-based updates (S4)
Flask-Limiter with Redis storage for per-user rate limiting plus pagination as the final cross-cutting layer, reusing the S2 auth context (S5)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions. Tests grew from 9 to 23 to 26 to 26 to 34 all-green passes, code grew from 124 to 499 lines, and model review scores climbed from 0.65 (S2) to 0.85 (S3) and 0.8 (S4) as the agent layered greenfield -> auth -> async integration -> refactor -> cross-cutting features, with SonarQube reporting zero bug deltas throughout. However the improvement was uneven: S2 introduced the story's main technical debt (hand-rolled JWT, no auth tests, monolith bloat), and the flat 0.673 convention score plus persistently identical violations show the agent refactored structure but never converged on style discipline.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-layered incremental build whose quality rose steadily across sessions, undercut only by Session 2's hand-rolled JWT and a fire-and-forget notification dispatch that left compounding debt the later refactor only partially repaid.
